correctness.rationale: For a one-point empirical sample, mean>0 forces zero downside deviation; so no admissible single observation. For exactly two equally weighted observations positive mean and nonzero downside force (-a,b), b>a>0. Let r=b/a: S=(r-1)/(r+1), Q=(r-1)/sqrt(2), both strictly increasing in r, proving no strict opposition. Exact rational direct moments of A=(-1,1,9), B=(-2,5,6) give common mean 3, variances 56/3 and 38/3, downside moments 1/3 and 4/3, thus S(A)<S(B) but Q(A)>Q(B). Padding with the common mean 3 proves this for every n>=3; checked n3..12 independently. For (-a,b,c) with one negative observation, variance=(a+mu)^2/2+(b-c)^2/6 explains upside-dispersion mechanism. One-negative-observation alternative Sortino denominator gives same rankings. Infinite n family follows exact algebra, not finite checks.

originality.rationale: Sharpe defines total dispersion; Sortino uses downside semivariance. Lien (2002) proves normal-law ranking agreement and identifies reversal under specified nonnormal Edgeworth-Sargan distributions; this already covers qualitative possibility and must not be advertised as new. value.rationale: The exact first possible sample size for disagreement is a natural invariant of two commonly used risk rankings, rather than an unmotivated selected portfolio. It exposes the minimal structural mechanism: one downside magnitude determines Sortino at a fixed mean, but imbalance of the two nonlosses independently affects Sharpe. The result is a mathematically informative boundary for finite empirical scoring, not a claim that three returns are enough for statistical selection.
